questions.prompt: What role do boundaries play in an architecture?

options.text: They act as firewalls against the harmful propagation of changes
They increase coupling between components
They define the database schema
They speed up the CPU

questions.explanation: Boundaries act as firewalls against harmful propagation of changes; components on each side change at different rates and for different reasons.

questions.prompt: When crossing boundaries, only data should cross — entity objects and database rows should not be passed across.
questions.explanation: Only data crosses boundaries, passed in the form most convenient for the inner circle; passing entities or DB rows would violate the Dependency Rule.

questions.prompt: From an architectural perspective, the database is...

options.text: A detail, not an architectural entity
The most important architectural entity
The same as the data model
A use case

questions.explanation: The database is a detail that does not rise to the level of an architectural element; however the data model (organizational structure of data) is architecturally significant.

questions.prompt: Which are listed options for organizing/packaging code?

options.text: Package by layer
Package by feature
Ports and adapters
Package by component

questions.explanation: The four packaging options presented are: package by layer, by feature, ports and adapters, and by component.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of the Humble Object pattern in testability?

options.text: To separate behaviors hard to test from behaviors easy to test
To remove all tests from the system
To merge the view and the model
To make the database faster

questions.explanation: The Humble Object separates hard-to-test behaviors (kept as simple as possible) from easy-to-test ones, and helps protect architectural boundaries; examples include DB gateways and data mappers.

questions.prompt: Tests are part of the system's architecture and also adhere to the Dependency Rule.
questions.explanation: Tests support development, but they are an integral component of the system and part of its architecture design; they also adhere to the Dependency Rule.

questions.prompt: What are described as the most basic components of a system?

options.text: UI, Logic, and Storage
Controller, Service, Repository
Producer, Filter, Consumer
Client, Broker, Server

questions.explanation: The most basic components of a system are UI, Logic, and Storage (e.g. the word-processor example).

questions.prompt: In the word-processor example, who defines and owns the API between WP Rules and the Language component?

options.text: The user (WP Rules), not the implementer (Language)
The implementer (Language), not the user
The database
The operating system

questions.explanation: WP Rules defines the API that Language implements; the API is defined and owned by the user, not by the implementer.

questions.prompt: What is the correct sequence for drawing architectural boundaries?

options.text: Partition into components, identify core-business components, then arrange dependencies to point toward the core business
Pick the database, then write the UI, then add business rules
Point all dependencies toward the database
Merge everything into a single component

questions.explanation: Drawing boundaries: partition the system into components, separate core-business components from non-core ones, and arrange code so dependencies point toward the core business.

questions.prompt: What is a disadvantage of organizing code 'by layer'?

options.text: As the software grows the layers become 'fat' and it is not tied to a specific business view
It perfectly reflects the domain
It makes every component independently deployable
It removes all dependencies between layers

questions.explanation: Package by layer is simple and common but layers grow fat as software grows, it isn't tied to a business view, and non-adjacent dependencies remain possible.

questions.prompt: What characterizes the ports-and-adapters packaging option?

options.text: Domain-specific code is well separated from implementation details, which depend on the domain (dependencies flow inward)
Implementation details own the domain code
Everything is grouped only by technical layer
The database is the innermost element

questions.explanation: Ports and adapters separate domain (inner) from implementation details (outer); the outer depends on the inner, with dependencies flowing inward.

questions.prompt: Packaging 'by feature' slices the system vertically so everything about a functionality lives in one package.
questions.explanation: Package by feature is vertical slicing that reflects the domain — everything about a functionality is in one package, though separation of details vs logic can be suboptimal.

questions.prompt: How should tests be designed to reduce their fragility?

options.text: They should depend as little as possible on volatile elements (e.g. test business rules without the GUI)
They should always go through the GUI
They should depend directly on the database schema
They should avoid the Dependency Rule

questions.explanation: To reduce fragility, tests should depend as little as possible on volatile elements — e.g. test business rules without the GUI; specific test APIs can avoid constraints.

questions.prompt: Which are given as examples of Humble Objects?

options.text: Database gateways
Data mappers (e.g. ORM)
Service listeners
Business rule interactors

questions.explanation: Humble Object examples include database gateways, data mappers (ORMs), and service listeners — hard-to-test boundary code kept as simple as possible.
